d: Running an already trained model: it outputs an answer for a new observation, and its weights don't change. The opposite of training. Inference time is how long the model takes to compute one answer, such as a chunk of actions.
What people do effortlessly — seeing, grasping, walking — turns out to be the hardest for machines, while chess and arithmetic come easily to a computer.

A control system built from modules with clear interfaces: perception, state estimation, planning, control. The modules run on rules and heuristics that an engineer writes and verifies. Lesson 0.1 calls this approach “Rules”.
An approach where a single neural network maps sensor data straight to commands, with no hand-written modules in between.
A failure the system does not report: the network confidently returns a wrong answer. A loud failure, where the system says “I can’t see” and stops, is safer: a human can be called in.
A multitude of rare situations: each one is uncommon, but together they make up a sizeable share. You cannot enumerate them in rules ahead of time.

A model that takes camera images and a command in words and directly outputs robot actions. The term was introduced by the authors of RT-2 (Google DeepMind, 2023), who fine-tuned an off-the-shelf vision-language model to output actions. Examples: RT-2, OpenVLA, π0; Helix and GR00T N1 split a VLA into a slow and a fast level.

One way to build a VLA: a slow vision-language model understands the scene and the command, and a fast policy turns its plan into motions. Helix, GR00T N1 and Gemini Robotics are built this way; RT-2 and π0 are a single model.
A function that maps an observation to a robot action at a fixed rate. It usually outputs targets for the controllers, not motor currents.
An independent coordinate you can control. For an arm, the degrees of freedom are its joints.
How many times the gearbox reduces speed and multiplies torque. The rotor inertia seen at the output grows as the square of the gear ratio.

How easily the actuator can be turned from the output side. Gearbox friction and reflected rotor inertia grow with the gear ratio, so a heavily geared actuator is nearly non-backdrivable: an external push does not turn the motor, and it passes impacts on rigidly.

The property of a backdrivable actuator to transmit force in both directions almost without distortion: an external force reaches the motor and can be estimated from current without a force sensor. The term comes from haptics. Transparent low-ratio actuators drive the legs of MIT Cheetah and Unitree robots.

A powerful motor with a low gear ratio, around 6:1. The actuator is backdrivable and transparent: it absorbs impacts softly, and force can be estimated from current. The legs of MIT Mini Cheetah and Unitree robots are built this way.

A gearbox in which an elliptical cam presses a flexible toothed ring against a rigid ring at two points. The flexible ring has two fewer teeth, so each cam revolution advances it by only two teeth: one compact stage gives a ratio of 30 to 160 with almost no backlash.
An actuator with a spring between the gearbox and the load: stable force control and protection from impacts, at the cost of bandwidth.
Sensors that measure the robot’s own state: joint angles and velocities, currents, body accelerations.
Sensors that look at the world around the robot: cameras, lidars, touch sensors.

The simplest sensor fusion: the gyroscope estimate with weight α plus the accelerometer estimate with weight 1 − α. The gyroscope is almost noise-free but drifts; the accelerometer does not drift but is noisy.
A slowly accumulating error in a sensor or an estimate, such as the angle from a gyroscope or the path from odometry.
The hierarchy of control loops: the lower the level, the faster it reacts — from a few hertz for the model that understands the command to tens of kilohertz for the current loop.
a: control hierarch(?:y|ies)|frequency ladder|ladder of (?:control )?frequencies|rate ladder|ladder of rates

d: The mismatch between how a robot behaves in the simulator and in real life. It often starts with the actuator: delays, friction, torque saturation.
A network trained on recordings of the real actuator to predict the torque it will deliver. It replaces the ideal model inside the simulator.
Computing the gripper pose from the joint angles. Pure geometry; there is always exactly one solution.
Finding the joint angles that put the gripper in the desired pose. There may be several solutions, one, or none.
The matrix that relates joint velocities to gripper velocity; its transpose relates forces at the gripper to joint torques.
A pose in which the Jacobian degenerates: the gripper loses the ability to move in some direction, for example along a fully extended arm.
A controller that pulls the joint toward its target like a spring (Kp times the error) and damps velocity like a damper (Kd times the velocity).
A torque term that, using a model of the arm, takes the arm’s weight off the controller. It removes the sag that a PD controller with finite stiffness cannot eliminate.
Control in which the arm behaves like a spring with a chosen stiffness: a position error turns into a moderate force rather than an impact.
Receding-horizon control: using a model, build a plan several seconds ahead, execute its beginning, then recompute the plan from the new state.
Working out where the robot is and what is around it from noisy, incomplete measurements.
A probability distribution over the robot’s possible states: the robot keeps not a point but where it most likely is and how sure it is.
State estimation with a Gaussian distribution in a “predict with the model → correct with the measurement” loop. The filter weighs the measurement using the noise levels Q and R.

t: Process and measurement noise (Q and R)
d: Q is how much to distrust the motion model, R is how much to distrust the measurement. Their ratio sets how much the filter trusts each measurement. Q is chosen with some margin.
State estimation with a set of weighted hypotheses, the particles. It keeps several hypotheses at once and survives ambiguity.
A test of whether the robot can find itself after being moved while its odometry noticed nothing.
Estimating displacement from wheel or joint rotation. Its error grows with distance travelled.
Building a map and estimating the pose against it at the same time. Without pose correction, walls on the map get duplicated.
A map made of cells, each holding the probability that the cell is occupied by an obstacle.
Shortest-path search that expands cells in order of their distance from the start.

Shortest-path search that expands cells by the sum of the path travelled so far and a heuristic estimate of what remains. With an admissible heuristic it finds the shortest path and usually expands fewer cells than Dijkstra.
An estimate of the remaining path to the goal. An admissible heuristic never overestimates the distance; it knows nothing about walls.
The space of all possible joint values of the robot. For an arm with n joints it is n-dimensional, and a grid over it does not fit in memory.
Random-tree planners: RRT quickly finds some path, RRT* straightens it toward the shortest one over time. Narrow passages are hard for them.
Training a policy on examples of an expert’s actions rather than on a reward.
Supervised learning on “observation → operator action” pairs. Simple and fast, and at the core of almost every robot model, but it suffers from distribution shift.
A recording of an expert performing the task: a sequence of observations and the expert’s actions.
The policy itself chooses which states it will see: a small error leads it to places where there were no demonstrations, and there it errs even more.
In the worst case, the error of behavior cloning over an episode of length T grows as εT², where ε is the per-step error rate. So validation accuracy guarantees nothing.
A feature that coincides with the correct action in the data but does not cause it. The policy learns to rely on it and fails when the coincidence disappears.
Iterative imitation learning: the policy drives on its own, the expert labels the states it reached, the new examples are added to all the old ones, and the policy is retrained.
A DAgger variant for humans: the expert does not label everything, but takes over control when they see danger.
The moment a human takes control away from the robot. The data gets the segment where the human drove, plus the signal “this is bad”.
Several networks trained on the same data with different initializations. Where there is plenty of data they agree; the spread of their answers is an estimate of uncertainty.
Several different correct actions in the same situation, for example passing the kettle on the left and on the right.
What regression with MSE learns: the average of all correct actions for a given observation. The average of two correct actions can be wrong.
Mean squared error. Its minimum is the mean of the examples.
The sum of absolute deviations. Its minimum is the median: when one side outweighs the other, L1 picks that side; with a tie the solution is not unique.
A peak of the action distribution — a distinct strategy, such as “pass on the left”.
A distribution made of several weighted Gaussians. The policy outputs the mixture parameters and samples one component.
A sequence of actions several steps ahead that the policy outputs in one go. The chunk holds on to the chosen strategy; the seams between chunks are reconciled, not averaged.
A generative model that learns to remove noise: it starts from pure noise and over several steps turns it into a sample from the data distribution.
One example drawn from a distribution: one generated point or one action chunk.
How fast the noise grows over the steps of the forward process. It sets the signal fraction ᾱ at every step.
A network that, given a noisy point and the step number, predicts the noise that was added. It shows where to move the point on the way back.
A diffusion sampler that adds fresh noise at every step. With few steps it loses the shape of the distribution.
A sampler with no fresh noise along the way: the same network, a deterministic path from noise to a point. Robots get by with 4–16 steps.

Conditional generation with a single network: during training the condition is sometimes dropped, during generation the conditional and unconditional outputs are blended. Strong guidance trades diversity for accuracy.
A policy that uses diffusion to generate a chunk of 16 future actions conditioned on the latest observations.
Predict a chunk several steps ahead, execute its beginning, and re-plan with new observations. Diffusion Policy predicts 16 and executes 8.
How many times the network refines the chunk from noise to finished actions. For robots, usually 1 to 16.
How many times a flow matching network outputs a velocity and the point is moved along it: one flow step is one network pass and the move x ← x + h·v. Robots usually take 4 to 10.
A unit of transformer input: a piece of an image, a word of the command, a state or an action, turned into a vector.
A mechanism in which each token mixes the values of other tokens with weights given by the similarity between its query and their keys.
The three projections of a token in attention: the query looks for what is needed, the key shows how well the token fits, the value is what the token contributes to the mix.
a: quer(?:y|ies), keys?,? and values?|keys? and values?|keys?(?= (?:vectors?|projections?))

d: A separate set of query, key and value projections. Different heads look at different features.
A table that forbids tokens from looking at certain other tokens: a blocked cell gets weight 0.
A vector added to a token so attention knows its place in the sequence. Without it, shuffling the tokens does not change the answer.
The stored keys and values of tokens already processed. It saves recomputation at inference.
The policy of the bimanual ALOHA robot: a transformer that outputs a chunk of 100 actions in one pass from the frames of four cameras. Trained with L1 and a CVAE encoder.
A human controlling the robot remotely. In ALOHA the operator moves the leader arms and the follower arms copy them joint by joint — that is how demonstrations are recorded.

A conditional variational autoencoder. In ACT, during training the CVAE encoder takes the joint positions and the operator's recorded chunk and outputs a 32-number vector z describing the operator's style, while the decoder — the policy itself — reconstructs the chunk from the images, joints and z. At inference the encoder is dropped and z = 0 is fed in.

Smoothing in ACT: the model is queried at every step, and the action is a weighted average of all predictions for that step from overlapping chunks. It copes poorly with latency and averages different strategies.

A way to stitch chunks together under inference latency: the next chunk is generated while the current one executes. Actions that will have executed by then are frozen; the rest are completed as a continuation of the old chunk.

Training a generative model by regressing a velocity field: the network learns to predict the velocity along a straight line from random noise to a random data point. Generation is a few Euler steps from noise to data.
A function that, at every point and every moment t, says where to move the point and how fast. The ideal field is the average of the velocities of all training lines through that point.
The simplest integration step: move the point by its velocity times the step length. On a curved path a large step cuts the corner.
Straightening the paths: a trained model generates “noise — result” pairs, and the same network is trained on those pairs. Their lines hardly cross, so one or two steps are enough.

A second, smaller set of weights in the same transformer as the VLM; in π0 about 300M parameters. The state and action tokens go through it, and it meets the VLM only in attention, reading the cached keys and values of the images and text. It builds the action chunk with flow matching.

A 2021 OpenAI model: two networks map an image and a caption into vectors in one space. Trained on 400 million image–caption pairs to guess which caption goes with which image, so an object can be found by a description in words.

Training on pairs: the similarity of the vectors of matching pairs (an image and its caption) is pushed up, and of non-matching pairs pushed down. That is how CLIP gets images and captions into one space.

A property of a model: if the input is shifted or rotated, the output shifts or rotates the same way. A fully convolutional network is shift-equivariant, which is why Transporter’s action map carries one demonstration to any spot on the table.

A 2020 Google model for pick-and-place tasks: the action is a per-pixel map over the top-down view, and the placement is found by template matching over 36 rotations. It learns from a handful to a few dozen demonstrations.
A 2021 two-stream model: CLIP answers what to pick, Transporter answers where. It understands words that never appeared in the robot’s demonstrations.
The simplest neural network: several fully connected layers, where each neuron receives all the outputs of the previous layer.
A pose in 3D: three coordinates and three rotation angles. A 6-DoF action sets where the gripper ends up and how it is oriented.
A 2022 model: from a voxel grid and a command in words it picks the next key gripper pose in 3D. One model learned 18 tasks in simulation and 7 tasks on a real arm.
A demonstration frame where joint velocities are near zero and the gripper is not changing state. PerAct predicts only the next keyframe pose; the path to it is built by a motion planner.
A cell of a 3D grid, the volumetric counterpart of a pixel. PerAct splits the cubic meter above the table into 100 × 100 × 100 voxels of 1 cm and picks the action as the highest-scoring voxel.

A transformer that reads a long input through a small set of learned latent vectors: cross-attention carries the input into the latents, and all-to-all attention runs only among them. Cost grows linearly with input length. PerAct uses 2048 latents for 8077 tokens.
A neural network trained on a huge corpus of text to predict the next token. It knows procedures from recipes and manuals and can write code, but it cannot see the robot or its surroundings.

An estimate of how good the current state is for the task: the expected sum of future rewards (more in lesson 5.1). If the reward is 1 for success and 0 for failure, the value equals the probability of success; this is how SayCan gets a skill's feasibility.

An estimate that a skill will succeed in the current scene. In SayCan it comes from the skill's value function: with a reward of 1 for success and 0 for failure, the value equals the probability of success. The SayCan paper calls it an affordance; VoxPoser's attraction map (an affordance map in that paper) is a different notion: it shows where to reach.
A 2022 Google planner: at every step it picks the robot skill with the highest product of usefulness from the language model and feasibility from the value function.
A model that answers, after a step, whether the skill succeeded. In Inner Monologue its answer is appended to the language model’s prompt.

A 2022 Google planner: the outcome of every step — success, visible objects, answers from the human — is written in words into the language model’s prompt, and it revises the plan without any fine-tuning.

A 2022 Google approach: the language model writes a Python program that calls the robot’s perception and control functions, computes coordinates and checks conditions. Missing functions the model writes itself.

A 2023 Stanford system: the language model writes code that builds 3D attraction and avoidance maps, a planner builds the gripper path over them and re-plans on the fly. Nothing is trained for the task.

VoxPoser's 3D grids with a score in every cell: on the attraction map, high values mark where to reach; on the avoidance map, what to stay away from. From a weighted sum of the maps the planner gets the path cost. The paper calls them value maps and the attraction map an affordance map; it has nothing to do with SayCan's feasibility.

A conditioning layer: from the command vector it computes a scale and a shift for every channel of the image features, F̂ = (1 + γ)·F + β. In RT-1 the FiLM layers sit inside EfficientNet and are initialized to the identity so as not to damage the pretrained weights.

A soft token selection module: a small network computes attention weights over the input tokens and assembles a few weighted sums from them. In RT-1 it compresses 81 image tokens to 8 and speeds up inference 2.4×.

A way to output a distribution over actions: the range of each dimension is split into equal intervals, bins, and the model predicts the probability of each bin as a class, while the robot gets the center of the chosen one. Bins over separate dimensions lose the links between dimensions; choosing them one by one (autoregression) brings the links back. RT-1 uses 256 bins for each of 11 dimensions.
a: action bins?|bins? of actions|action discretization|actions? as tokens?|action tokens?|(?<=called\s)bins

d: An experiment that removes or replaces one part of the system to measure its contribution: no pretraining, no frame history, half the data. RT-1’s ablations showed that data diversity matters more than data volume.

The number of distinct tasks, objects and environments in a dataset, as opposed to the number of episodes. By RT-1’s ablations, dropping 25% of the tasks cost as much generalization as dropping 49% of the episodes.

A model that takes an image and text and answers in text: an image encoder, a projector and a language model. LLaVA and PaliGemma are assembled from off-the-shelf parts; RT-2, π0 and the other models of Part 3 are built on VLMs.

A transformer for images (Google, 2021): the image is cut into 16 × 16 patches, a linear layer turns each patch into a token, a position vector is added, then ordinary attention blocks follow. The gains of large ViTs show only on hundreds of millions of images.

A square piece of an image, for example 16 × 16 pixels, that is flattened into a vector and turned into a transformer token. A 224 × 224 image gives 196 patches; without position vectors, the set of patches is an unordered bag to attention.

A trainable layer between the image encoder and the language model: it maps the encoder’s tokens into the dimension of word embeddings. In LLaVA it is one matrix, in LLaVA-1.5 and OpenVLA a two-layer MLP, in PaliGemma a linear layer initialized to zero.

An attention mask in which the input tokens — image and prompt — see each other in full, while the answer tokens see only what comes before them. PaliGemma is built this way; a plain causal mask over the image and prompt works worse.

The part of a model that is not updated during training. LLaVA keeps the CLIP encoder frozen always, and the language model frozen in the first stage, when only the projector learns; PaliGemma freezes nothing.

A model trained on data from many robots or tasks works better on a specific robot than a model trained on that robot’s data alone. The opposite is negative transfer: data from other robots gets in the way.

A storage format for robot episodes: observations, actions and metadata step by step in tfrecord files. It accommodates different action spaces and sensor sets, which is why Open X-Embodiment is assembled in it.

Translating the model’s output back from the shared normalized format into the units of a specific robot: grid cells, millimeters, velocities. The same token string is read by every robot in its own way.
The model lacks the capacity or the training steps to fit all the data: it performs poorly even on the training set. That is how the authors explain RT-1-X losing on large datasets.
The shares of datasets when training on a mixture: the probability that an example for a batch is drawn from each set. Proportional to size, the big sets dominate; the weights are tuned by hand.

A person who controls the robot by hand — with a controller, a joystick or a copy of the arm — and thereby records the demonstrations the network later learns from. How such control works is covered in lesson 1.7.

The scripted planner in the course labs: it knows the map and the route and outputs the correct steering. It records the demonstrations the policy learns from, and in DAgger it labels the frames the policy drove into.
In the DAgger papers — whoever knows the correct action: a human or a program. In the course labs the expert is the teacher; in the “You are the expert” task of lesson 1.2 it is you.
The robot tries acting on its own and learns from a numeric score of its attempts — the reward: it repeats more often whatever is followed by a higher reward.
One training pass over all the training examples.
The number the network drives down during training: how far its answers are from the examples. For instance, the mean squared error (MSE).
The rotational force with which the motor turns the joint. Measured in newton-meters (N·m): 1 N·m is a force of 1 newton on a 1 m lever.
A sensor made of a gyroscope and an accelerometer: it measures the rotation and acceleration of the body, and the robot’s tilt is estimated from it.

Attention in which the queries come from one sequence of tokens and the keys and values from another. That is how the 100 decoder queries of ACT read the camera tokens, and the Perceiver latents in PerAct read a million voxels.

A 2023 Google DeepMind VLA: the off-the-shelf vision-language models PaLI-X (up to 55 billion parameters) and PaLM-E (12 billion), fine-tuned to output the robot action as a string of eight integers — as vocabulary tokens. It generalizes to new objects, backgrounds and settings about twice as well as RT-1.

Fine-tuning a pretrained model on new data together with the original data: in RT-2, robot demonstrations in every batch alongside the VLM’s web data. It keeps the model from forgetting what it knew. In RT-2 it clearly helped the 55B model (63% vs 52%), but barely the 5B one (44% vs 42%).

Losing old skills while training on a new task: the weights rearrange for the new data, and nobody checks the old skills any more. In lesson 3.3 a model fine-tuned on actions alone forgets how to name the color in an image.

What the model does without a single demonstration of that kind, carrying knowledge over from pretraining: for RT-2, moving objects to digits and icons, to a cup of the same color, to the person wearing glasses, understanding commands in other languages.
Continuing to train a ready model on a small dataset for the target task, starting from its weights rather than random ones. This is how a pretrained model is adapted to a task or to your own robot.
Learnable tokens in Octo that read the task and observation tokens but are read by nobody. Their output goes to the action head, so a new head can be added without touching the model’s backbone.

A small network on top of the model’s backbone that turns its output into action numbers: by regression, tokens or diffusion. The head determines what the model does when there are several correct actions.

A fine-tuning method: the weight matrix W is frozen, and a low-rank update B·A of rank r is learned alongside it. For a large matrix of side d, about 2r/d of the parameters are trained; after training the update is added to W, and the model runs at its original speed.
Storing model weights in fewer bits, for example 8 or 4 instead of 16: the model takes less memory at almost the same accuracy.

A 2024 Physical Intelligence model: the 3-billion-parameter vision-language model PaliGemma and a 300-million action expert in a single transformer. In 10 steps of flow matching it builds a chunk of 50 continuous actions, and the robots receive commands 50 times per second.

The first stage of training a large model, on a large and diverse dataset covering many tasks: the model learns general things, for example what objects look like. In RT-1 the network that reads the frames is pretrained this way on ImageNet.
Fine-tuning an already trained model on a smaller, curated set of clean recordings of a specific task. For π0: from 5 to 100-plus hours of recordings of one task.

Decomposes a sequence of numbers into a sum of cosines of different frequencies. For a smooth signal almost everything is concentrated in a few low frequencies, which is why the transform is used for compression — in JPEG and in the FAST tokenizer.
A 2025 action tokenizer: the chunk is compressed with a cosine transform, rounding and BPE, and the token count drops several-fold — one second of folding a T-shirt takes 53 tokens instead of 700.

The upper level of a dual-system controller: a large vision-language model that, several times per second, understands the scene and the request and decides what to do. In Helix a 7-billion-parameter model at 7–9 Hz; in GR00T N1, Eagle-2 at 10 Hz.

The lower level of a dual system: a small policy that, hundreds of times per second, takes the latest frame and the slow system’s latest output and issues commands to the arms. In Helix 80 million parameters at 200 Hz; in GR00T N1, a DiT at 120 Hz.

The third, fastest level of Helix 02: a 10-million-parameter network that, 1000 times per second, turns the joint state into actuator commands and keeps the whole body balanced. Trained in simulation, it replaced 109,504 lines of C++ code.

A set of numbers one part of a network uses to pass what it understood to another; the meaning of the numbers is not set in advance but emerges during training. In Helix the slow system passes one such vector to the fast one.

A model that does not move the robot itself: it plans the steps, calls tools and hands the steps to the executor. In Gemini Robotics 1.5 the orchestrator Gemini Robotics-ER passes steps to the VLA in plain words.

Understanding the space and physics of the scene the way a robot needs it: where the objects are, where to grab them, where to guide the gripper. That is what Google DeepMind calls the skills of the Gemini Robotics-ER model.
A formula linking model quality to scale: data volume, model size, compute. Usually a power law: the error falls as β·X^−α, which is a straight line on log-log axes.

In Lin et al. — one minus the policy’s normalized score on new environments and objects, the share of points left on the table. It is this gap that falls as a power law in the number of environments, objects and environment–object pairs.

An estimate of how far robot data lags behind language model data: the corpus is converted into the time a human would need to read it — on the order of 100,000 years, versus about a year of recordings in the largest robot datasets. A thought experiment by Kevin Black, repeated by Ken Goldberg.

“Good old-fashioned engineering” — Ken Goldberg’s name for model-based methods: Kalman filters, inverse kinematics, motion planning. He proposes combining them with learned models so that robots can work and collect data along the way.
One attempt at the task from start to finish — the unit of counting in robot datasets. The recorded sequence of frames, states and actions of an episode is called a trajectory.
A copy of the robot arm that the operator moves with their own hands; its joint angles are sent to the robot one-to-one, with no inverse kinematics. ALOHA and GELLO are built this way.
Transferring human motion to a robot with a different body: for example, choosing the robot’s finger angles so that its fingertips, or the vectors between keypoints of the hand, match the human’s.

A device worn on the body: its links run along the person’s arms, angle sensors sit at their joints, and the angles are sent to the robot. AirExo is for two manipulator arms, HOMIE is a cockpit for a humanoid.

A gripper with a camera that a person holds in their hand and uses to do the task themselves, without the robot; the same gripper with the same camera is then mounted on the robot. UMI is the example.

The shared rules for recording every episode of a dataset: how to set up the scene and calibrate the cameras, how to choose the task, when to change the setting, how to mark success. DROID uses one protocol across 13 institutions, so recordings from different collectors are compatible.
Where the camera stands and where it looks. Viewpoint diversity in the data teaches the policy not to depend on how the camera was placed; DROID has 1,417 of them.

How much the learned policy’s actions differ from the expert’s in the same states. It grows when the operator acts differently in identical situations; one of the two data quality properties in Belkhale et al.
How varied the next states are for the same state and action — the noise of the world itself. Unlike the spread in the operator’s actions, it widens the data in a useful way.

How much knowing one quantity tells you about another: I(S; A) = H(A) − H(A | S). For robot data it is high when actions are diverse yet easy to predict from the state; the DemInf demonstration selection builds on this.

Checking the dataset and removing harmful episodes: failed, contradictory, with pauses and jerks. A small verified set is often better than a large unverified one: in AgiBot World, 528 verified trajectories scored 0.59 against 0.41.

Training one model on several kinds of data and tasks at once in a shared mixture. For π0.5, recordings of mobile robots in homes are only 2.4% of the first-stage examples; the rest is other robots, web data and step captions.
A short command in words that the robot completes in a few seconds, such as “pick up the cutting board”. π0.5 first names the subtask itself, then outputs actions that depend on it alone.
A way to train a VLA without damaging the vision-language model’s knowledge: it learns actions as FAST tokens and keeps learning on web data, while the action expert’s gradient does not flow into it.
An operation in which a quantity takes part in the forward pass as usual but is treated as a constant in the backward pass: no gradient flows through it.
The model first writes out its reasoning, then the answer. In ECoT, before every action the VLA writes the plan, the subtask, the motion in words, the gripper position and the object bounding boxes.

How much better an action is than what the agent usually does in that state: A(s, a) = Q(s, a) − V(s). For the action a deterministic policy would pick itself it is zero; switching to actions with positive advantage does not make the policy worse. π*0.6 writes “Advantage: positive” into the model’s input when the advantage is above a threshold.
Video shot by a camera on a person’s head or glasses: the frame shows what they see and their own hands. An example is Ego4D: 3,670 hours of the everyday life of 931 people.

The body a system acts in the world with: a five-fingered hand for a human, a two-link arm with a gripper for Ada. Data from different embodiments can be trained in one model if it is brought to a common description.

The difference between the body that showed the action and the body that has to repeat it: link lengths, fingers instead of a gripper, speed, how it looks in the frame. The main difficulty of training a robot on human video.

A model that guesses, from the frames before and after, which action happened in between. It is easier to train than a policy because it also sees what happened next; it is used to label action-free video (VPT, GR00T N1).

A code from a vocabulary into which the model compresses the change between two video frames so that the second frame can be reconstructed from the first frame and the code. It serves as the action for unlabeled video; in GR00T N1 it is shared by humans and robots.

An internal vector of the policy’s upper level from which the hand’s path several seconds ahead is predicted. In MimicPlay it is learned from video of human play, and the lower level turns it into robot actions.

A program that computes step by step how the robot and objects move: joint forces, contacts, falls. The physics engine computes the mechanics, the renderer draws the camera image. Examples: MuJoCo, Isaac Lab, Genesis.

Fitting model parameters to measurements of the real robot — masses, friction, delays — so the simulator behaves like it. Not everything can be measured this way: backlash, wear and compliance remain.

Training in a simulator where every scene randomly varies the properties the simulator reproduces poorly: textures, lighting, camera, masses, friction. The goal is for the real world to look to the model like just another variant. You randomize what the model should be indifferent to.
The ratio of successful demonstration generation attempts to their total number. In MimicGen every generated trajectory is executed in the simulator and kept only if the task is completed.

A copy of the real workplace in the simulator, with objects placed where the robot’s camera measured them. In DexMimicGen trajectories were generated in the twin, and only the successful ones were executed on the real humanoid.

A training set for one model assembled from several sources — recordings of your own robot, other robots, simulation, human video, web data — where each source has a set share in the training batches.

GR00T N1’s way of arranging data in layers: at the bottom web data and human video — the most of it, but farthest from the robot; in the middle simulation and generated video; at the top recordings of real robots — the least, but with their actions.

A loop in which working robots or cars record their attempts, failures are labeled and fed back into training, the next model works better and in more places, and there are more recordings. Tesla calls it the data engine; π*0.6 calls it RECAP.
A new model runs on the car or robot alongside the active one: it computes its own answers but does not control anything. Its disagreements reveal errors without putting hardware or people at risk.
The number the agent receives from the environment after every step: how well it went. The reward says what to achieve, not how; the agent’s goal is the highest expected sum of rewards.

The sum of future rewards from step t, where the reward k steps ahead is multiplied by γ to the power k: G_t = r_{t+1} + γ r_{t+2} + γ² r_{t+3} + … The agent picks actions so that the expected return is highest.

A number γ between 0 and 1 in the return: a reward one step ahead weighs γ times less than the same reward now. It sets how far the agent looks: the weight of a reward halves in 1 step at γ = 0.5 and in about 69 steps at γ = 0.99.

The link between the value of a state and the values of the next ones: the value equals the expected reward for the step plus the discounted value of the state the step leads to. For the optimal policy the best action is taken: V*(s) = max_a [r + γ V*(s′)].

A dynamic programming algorithm: start from any value estimates and recompute all states by the Bellman equation with a max over actions until the estimates stop changing. It needs a model of the environment — where actions lead and what rewards they give.

A way to choose actions during training: with probability 1 − ε the best by current estimates, with probability ε a random one. The agent keeps exploring and may find an action better than the one that currently looks best.

The expected return if you take action a in state s and then follow the policy: Q(s, a). The state value V(s) is the same but with the action the policy itself would pick. Choosing an action from Q is simple: take the one with the larger Q.

A policy that outputs not a single action but a distribution: for continuous steering, the mean and spread of a normal distribution. The randomness is needed for exploration: the robot tries actions near the mean and learns which are better.

The direction in the policy’s weight space in which the expected return grows fastest. It is estimated from runs: every action taken is nudged with a weight equal to the return or advantage that followed it (the REINFORCE method and its descendants).

A number b(s) subtracted from the return in the policy gradient. If it depends only on the state, the mean gradient direction is unchanged while the variance drops. Usually it is the value V(s) — and then the action’s weight becomes the advantage.

An advantage estimator (Schulman et al., 2015): the sum of one-step value errors δ with weights (γλ)^k. At λ = 0 it is one step and full trust in the critic, at λ = 1 the full return minus the value; intermediate λ trade off bias and variance.

A limit on how much the new policy may differ from the old one in a single update; in TRPO, the mean KL divergence is at most δ = 0.01. It is needed because the gradient estimate is only valid near the policy that collected the data.

A policy gradient method (Schulman et al., 2017): an objective with the ratio of new to old policy probabilities clipped to 1 ± ε keeps one update from taking the policy too far, so several epochs can be run over one rollout batch. The standard for learning to walk in simulation.

Learning only from experience collected by the current version of the policy: after an update that experience describes a different policy and is thrown away. REINFORCE, TRPO and PPO work this way; they need many interaction steps.

Learning from transitions collected by a different policy, including past versions of your own: Q-learning, DQN, DDPG, TD3 and SAC learn this way. It lets you keep experience in a replay buffer and reuse every step many times.

A store of transitions (state, action, reward, next state) from which a random batch is drawn at every training step. Every transition teaches many times, and the random batch breaks the correlation between neighboring steps. It first appeared in DQN.

A pair of networks trained together: the actor chooses the action (or a distribution over actions), and the critic estimates how good it is. In PPO the critic predicts the state value V(s), which is used to compute the advantage; in DDPG, TD3 and SAC the critic estimates the action value Q(s, a) and tells the actor which way to shift the action.

Systematic inflation of values in Q-learning: the max over noisy estimates is on average larger than the truth, and the policy itself seeks out the actions where the critic erred upward. TD3 and SAC fight it by taking the smaller of two Q-functions.

Reinforcement learning where the policy’s entropy, weighted by α — the temperature — is added to the reward: solve the task while acting as randomly as possible. The basis of SAC; in its second version α tunes itself, holding the entropy at the target −dim A. The SAC policy is a single Gaussian with one peak: it widens its spread but does not split probability between two equally good actions.

The robot model the simulator knows: masses and dimensions from the drawings, friction from the datasheet, a motor that delivers exactly the requested torque with no delay. The real robot always differs from it a little.

The time from the policy’s decision until the actuator starts executing it (and the sensor reports the result). Simulators often have none; on Minitaur it is 15–19 ms. It breaks the feedback loop: the policy corrects an error that is no longer there.

Training a policy in a simulator where every episode randomly varies the physical parameters — masses, friction, latency, motor strength — so that it works across the whole distribution of worlds, and therefore on the real robot. The price is caution and speed.

Randomization ranges start from the calibrated world and widen on their own: a boundary moves outward if the policy performs at least as well as the upper threshold there, and back if worse than the lower one. OpenAI, 2019, the Rubik’s cube.
Training from easy to hard: the task is first solved under easy conditions, and hard ones are added when the policy is ready for them. ADR and the terrain levels of Rudin et al. work this way.

The ability of a policy with memory to work out, while running, which world it is in and adapt without updating its weights. At OpenAI it emerged on its own from training on a wide distribution of worlds.

Reinforcement learning from pre-collected “state, action, reward, next state” transitions only — no new attempts during training; the policy is run once training is over. The goal is a policy better than the one that collected the data.
Those who collected the data for offline RL — operators and past versions of the policy, together: the logs record how they acted. Denoted π_β.

Unrealistic Q estimates for state–action pairs absent from the data (Fujimoto et al., 2018). Together with the max in the Q-learning target they produce persistent overestimation that, without new attempts, nothing can correct.

An offline RL method (Kumar et al., 2020): a penalty α·(log Σ exp Q(s, a′) − Q(s, a from the data)) is added to the Bellman error, pushing down high estimates for actions outside the data. With a large enough α the expected estimate of the policy is no higher than the truth.

An offline RL method (Kostrikov, Nair, Levine, 2021) that never evaluates actions outside the data: V(s) is an expectile of the Q estimates of recorded actions, the target value for Q is r + γV(s′), and the policy is imitation learning weighted by exp(β·(Q − V)).

A distribution statistic that minimizes the asymmetric squared error |τ − 1(u < 0)|·u². At τ = 0.5 it equals the mean; as τ approaches 1 it approaches the maximum — but only over the values seen in the data.

A policy that in the simulator receives as input what the real robot will not have: hidden world parameters, the exact map, contacts. With full information it learns fast, then serves as a teacher for a student that uses sensors only; on the robot only the student runs.

A property of the world the correct action depends on but the sensors do not show directly: floor friction, payload mass, motor strength. In the simulator it is known; on the robot it has to be inferred from the motion history.

How hard the floor can push the wheel along and sideways before it starts slipping. In the labs of lesson 5.5 it is the number μ: carpet 1, tile 0.7, wet floor 0.45; it limits braking and lateral acceleration in turns.

A network that estimates the hidden world parameters from the history of the robot’s recent states and actions (in RMA a compressed vector of 8 numbers) and feeds the estimate to the base policy. It is trained by regression on its own runs in the simulator; on the robot it updates the estimate in a fraction of a second.

A program or model that checks at run time whether a step succeeded and raises an alarm on failure. It turns silent failures into loud ones, but errs in both directions itself: it misses failures and raises false alarms.
A detector alarm on a step or run that actually succeeded. The lower the alarm threshold, the fewer missed failures and the more false alarms; each one is an unnecessary call to a human.

How long the robot works on average from one call to a human until the next: operating time divided by the number of interventions. It cannot exceed operating time divided by the number of real failures.

A way to pick a threshold from labeled calibration examples so that the correct answer lands in the prediction set with probability at least 1 − ε — on average over scenarios from the same distribution, with any model. In KnowNo the robot uses it to decide whether to act or ask for help.
All options whose score is at or above the threshold from conformal calibration. In KnowNo: one option — the robot acts; more than one — it asks the human which is right.
If n independent runs produced no failure, then with 95% confidence the failure rate is below roughly 3/n: 99% takes about 300 successful runs in a row, 99.9% about 3000.

A module that watches the control system’s commands at run time and, if a command leads to a safety violation, changes it as little as possible (Hsu, Hu, Fisac, 2023). It is designed without knowledge of the task, so it sits on top of any policy, including a learned one.

A function of the state h that is non-negative in the safe set and zero on its boundary, such that at every point there is a command for which ḣ ≥ −α(h) (Ames et al., 2019). If this condition holds, the system never leaves the safe set.
The set of states in which the system is considered safe — for example, all robot positions farther than a given distance from an obstacle. Usually written as {x : h(x) ≥ 0}.
A property of a set: if the system is in it at some moment, it stays in it at all later moments. Ames et al. define safety as forward invariance of the safe set.

A program synthesized in advance from a formal safety specification that at every step leaves the agent only the safe discrete actions (a shield before the agent) or replaces a chosen unsafe action with a safe one (a shield after the agent) (Alshiekh et al., 2017).

The conditions under which the system must operate safely and for which its guarantees hold: for a safety filter — model accuracy, perception error, completeness of the obstacle map. The term comes from the SAE J3016 standard.

A network whose output is added to the command of an existing controller: action = controller + correction. The last layer of the correction is zeroed at the start, so before training it changes nothing; the network learns only what the controller’s model does not know (Silver et al.; Johannink et al., 2018).

A pick-and-drop system for unfamiliar homes (New York University and Meta, 2024), assembled with no fine-tuning: open neural networks find the object and choose the grasp, classical methods plan the base path (A*) and guide the arm. 58.5% of tasks in cluttered homes, 82.4% after tidying up.
A neural network that, from a single depth camera’s point cloud, outputs a set of grasp poses for a two-finger gripper in 100 ms (Fang et al., 2023). A classical arm motion planner executes the pose.

The position and orientation at which the gripper should close on the object; for a two-finger gripper the opening width is added. A network or a rule picks it, and a planner and controller bring the arm to it.

A Google DeepMind policy (2023) whose goal is given as a sketch of the gripper path over the camera frame: time is encoded by one color, height by another, circles mark the grasp. The sketch is drawn by a person, built from video, or written by a language model. The sketch is executed by a learned policy built like RT-1, not by a classical controller.

A reinforcement learning system on a real robot (Luo et al., 2024): RLPD with demonstration and experience buffers, an image-based reward classifier, and human takeover whose steps go into both buffers. 100% success in 1–2.5 hours on assembly and insertion tasks.

A network that answers from a camera frame whether the task is done; it gives a sparse reward of 1 at the end of a successful attempt and 0 otherwise. In HIL-SERL it is trained on ~200 success frames and ~1000 failure frames, about 5 minutes of recording.

A SAC variant (Ball, Smith, Kostrikov, Levine, 2023) for online learning with pre-collected data: symmetric sampling, layer normalization in the critic, and many updates per step with an ensemble of critics. The basis of SERL and HIL-SERL.

Every training batch is drawn half from the buffer of pre-collected data (demonstrations and corrections), half from the robot’s experience buffer. Rare corrections are seen often, and overestimation does not run away.

A method for training a VLA with reinforcement learning (π*0.6, Physical Intelligence, 2025): a value function from the robot’s own attempts, the advantage of every step is compared with a threshold, and the label “Advantage: positive / negative” is written into the model’s input; operator corrections are always positive; at run time positive is written in.

A way to extract an improved policy without weights or a policy gradient: the model is trained on all the data by ordinary supervised learning, and its input gets an indicator of whether the action is better than usual. At β = 1 the improved policy equals the conditional distribution π(a | I = 1, o).
The policy outputs target positions, and the controller brings the joint there on its own; execution misses do not accumulate, and a late command does less harm.
The policy outputs increments or velocities; the controller counts them from the actual position, so misses add up and latency drifts the robot off the route.

A method for automatic selection of demonstrations (Hejna et al., 2025): it scores each episode by its contribution to the mutual information between the states and actions of the dataset. Episodes where the action is easy to predict from the state, while actions across the dataset are diverse, get a high score; episodes with a low score are dropped entirely. The method assumes all demonstrations are successful and scores episodes with pauses highly, so failures and pauses are filtered out separately.

Sensors or cameras with markers that record the movements of the body and fingers. In DexCap these are gloves with magnetic sensors in the fingertips, in AgiBot World it is recording the operator's whole-body movements for teleoperation, and in Dactyl it is cameras tracking markers on the fingers of the robot hand.

An attention mask under which each token sees itself and the tokens to its left, but not the following ones. This is how a language model is trained: the next word is predicted without looking ahead in the sentence.

A mask that opens and closes attention for whole blocks of tokens: within a block tokens see each other, between blocks only the earlier ones. π0 has three blocks: frames and command, state, actions. The observation does not see the actions, so its keys and values are computed once per chunk and kept in the KV cache.
A large model pretrained on a broad and diverse dataset covering many tasks, applied to new tasks directly or after a short fine-tuning. Part 3 of the course is about such models for robots.

The time from a captured frame to the first command built from it: model inference plus the network path. It shows how long the robot waits for a response to what it saw; for Gemini Robotics about 250 ms.

How much time has passed since the frame from which the currently executed command was built. For the first command of a chunk it equals the latency, and it grows until the next chunk arrives: with a 7 Hz model, from 143 to 286 ms.

π0.6 adapted for reinforcement learning (Physical Intelligence, 2025): the same architecture, but the input carries an "Advantage: positive/negative" label, and the model is trained with RECAP, first on a mixture of data from many tasks and robots, then for each task on the robot's own attempts.
All the steps an on-policy method like PPO collects with the current policy before one update; several epochs of minibatches are run over it, and then it is discarded.
The number y = r + γ·max Q(s′, a′) toward which the estimate Q(s, a) is pulled; it is computed by the target network, and TD3 and SAC take the smaller of two Q′.
The entropy level SAC maintains by tuning α; by default −dim A, for Ada's arm −2.

Walking control that isn't designed by hand but obtained by reinforcement learning in a simulator. The policy outputs target joint angles 50 times a second, PD controllers turn them into torques, thousands of copies of the robot collect experience, and the reward is a sum of many terms. This is how Hwangbo et al. (2019) and Rudin et al. (2021) trained ANYmal, and Radosavovic et al. (2024) the Digit humanoid.

The desired body velocities (forward, sideways, turning) that a walking policy receives as input. In training, each copy gets its own random command: for the whole episode in Rudin et al., a new one every 10 s in Radosavovic et al. If training uses a single command, the policy doesn't learn to follow others.

In training for walking, the reward per step is a weighted sum of terms. Some reward tracking the command (through a bounded kernel exp(−error²/0.25)) and long steps; others penalize bouncing, body rocking, joint torques and accelerations, changes of the joint targets and collisions. Rudin et al. use nine terms, Margolis and Agrawal eighteen, and none of them specifies the gait.

Behavior that collects reward without solving the task. A policy rewarded only for forward speed lies down and pushes itself along the floor with its legs, and one with only a fall penalty speeds up and falls. Such loopholes are closed with terms that describe how exactly to move and by ending the episode on a fall.

Training in which thousands of copies of a robot step simultaneously on one GPU and the data never leaves its memory (Isaac Gym). In Rudin et al., 4,096 copies making 24 steps per update and 1,500 updates took under 20 minutes. There can also be too many copies: with the same rollout batch, each one gets fewer than 25 consecutive steps, and GAE stops working.

Training without a gradient: at each update, the policy parameters are randomly perturbed in N directions, each version is tried in episodes, and the parameters shift toward the directions with higher reward (Mania, Guy, Recht, 2018). The more copies per update, the more accurate the step, but with a shared episode budget, the fewer updates there are.

A policy with a history of observations and actions in its input adjusts its behavior to the floor, a load or a push without changing its weights. The history changes, not the network, just as a language model changes its answer based on a prompt. In Radosavovic et al., this is a causal transformer over 16 “observation, action” pairs.

Training a policy with reinforcement learning in a physics simulation where the reward is computed from a recording of human motion: for closeness to the frame of the recording (tracking, DeepMimic) or for the policy's transitions being indistinguishable from the recorded ones (AMP). The policy outputs target angles for PD controllers, and balance and the response to pushes come from the simulation.

Motion imitation with a reward for the pose's closeness to the frame of the recording at the same phase: joint angles and velocities, hand and foot positions, the center of mass (DeepMimic). The policy is called a tracker. Tracking is accurate but tied to the recording's tempo: to walk faster, you need a different recording.

A number φ from 0 to 1 in the input of a DeepMimic policy that shows where the recording is now: 0 is its start and 1 its end, and for cyclic motions it goes back to 0 after the end. The phase tells which frame to compare the pose with and ties the policy to the recording's tempo.

A training episode starts from a random frame of the recording, with its pose and velocities, rather than from the same pose every time. This way, the policy sees the late phases of the motion from the very first episodes. Without RSI, the DeepMimic character learned a hop instead of a backflip, and ExBody's training didn't work at all.

An episode ends when the torso or the head touches the floor, and the reward for the rest of it is zero. This is both a fall penalty and a filter on experience: lying-down states don't pile up in it. For walking, it barely changes the result; for a backflip, it's decisive.

Adversarial motion priors (Peng et al., 2021): a discriminator learns to tell transitions from the recordings from the policy's transitions, and the policy gets a style reward max[0, 1 − 0.25(D − 1)²] together with a task reward. There's no phase and no choice of recording, so dozens of unlabeled recordings go into training, and the gait changes with the command.

A network that looks at a sample and answers whether it's real or produced by a model. In AMP, the discriminator scores a transition between two neighboring states: from a recording (a score of 1) or from the policy (−1). It learns along with the policy, and its score serves as the policy's style reward.

A weakness of adversarial models: out of a dataset with different variants, the model reproduces only some and loses the other modes. An AMP policy trained on a large dataset of recordings imitates only a small subset of the motions.

A whole-body policy that gets the target frame of a motion in its input as part of the command and reproduces any recording fed to it frame by frame, including the pose of a person in front of a camera in real time. It needs neither a phase nor the recording's number, so one network replaces the trackers of individual recordings. This is how H2O and OmniH2O work.

Transferring the skill of one policy to another: the student learns to repeat the teacher's actions instead of solving the task from scratch. Usually the teacher sees the robot's full state in the simulator, while the student has only sensors, and the student is trained with DAgger: it acts on its own, and the teacher labels its states. This is how the OmniH2O and HOVER students were obtained.

A way of specifying motion to a whole-body policy: which body parts are given and by what, point positions, joint angles or pelvis motion. ExBody gives the arm angles and the pelvis motion, H2O gives points across the whole body, and OmniH2O only the head and hands. A policy trained for a single mode is called a specialist.

A set of bits, one for each part of the command: the parts that are on are given, and the ones that are off arrive as zeros. In HOVER, the mask is chosen at random at the start of each training episode, so one policy understands any combination of parts and works in all command modes.

A single policy for all command modes, trained with a random command mask, unlike a specialist, which is trained in one mode. In HOVER, the generalist beats specialists trained with reinforcement learning. In the lab of lesson 6.3, a specialist trained by the same teacher is more accurate in its own mode but errs several times more in another, while the generalist switches modes on the move.

A correction to the simulator learned from data recorded on the real robot: given the state and the action, it outputs an addition to the action with which the simulator, starting from the recorded state, ends up where the robot did (ASAP). The policy is fine-tuned in the simulator with the correction and runs on the robot without it.

A way to give a diffusion model a task at inference without new training: the task is written as a differentiable cost of the plan, and at each denoising step the cost's gradient shifts the plan toward meeting it. Unlike with classifier-free guidance, the model doesn't need to be trained with a condition. This is how BeyondMimic steers a humanoid by joystick, to a point and around an obstacle.

d: A depth camera: together with the color image (RGB) it gives the distance to every pixel (D, depth). Color and depth are turned into a point cloud and a voxel grid. How the camera measures depth is shown in the diagram in lesson 0.2.
